name: Account & identity pivoting
description: Turn one account or handle into the person's other accounts, and know when a shared username is NOT the same person.
author: VINEYARD
overview:
Account & identity pivoting — from one handle or email to the accounts behind the same person,
without over-merging strangers who happen to share a name.

Use this when the analyst has a username, email, or profile and wants "where else is this person".
Load the section for the lead you are holding:
  - "from-handle"  - a username: spreading it across platforms
  - "from-email"   - an address: the handles, keys and documents behind it
  - "from-profile" - one profile page: mining it for every pivot it carries
  - "discriminate" - a candidate pair with a gap: the check that would settle it
  - "corroborate"  - deciding whether two accounts are one person

Read "corroborate" first: the whole risk here is collapsing two people into one node. A wrong merge
is not a missing fact, it is a false one, and it survives into every conclusion drawn afterwards.

THREE RULES THAT APPLY TO EVERY SECTION, so they are not repeated in each:

1. LOOP, DO NOT SWEEP ONCE. A pass produces candidates; a candidate has a gap; a gap names a check
   ("discriminate"); the check produces evidence, which produces new candidates. Keep going while a
   pass still adds something — an account nobody had, a pair settled, a pair ruled out. Stop when
   the frontier is empty or the budget is spent, and say WHICH of the two. A tidy report is not the
   goal; a closed question is. While a candidate pair has an open gap and something installed here
   could close it, you are not finished.

2. WHAT YOUR OWN KNOWLEDGE IS FOR. Use it freely to JUDGE — how common a string is, what a name
   suggests, which check is worth running next. Judging is why you are here instead of a scoring
   table. It never becomes a node or an edge on its own: never assert that an account exists, or
   that a handle is taken, from memory — nor from a string you composed, which is the same failure
   wearing a method. On the canvas, a profile URL you recalled and one a tool returned are
   indistinguishable. Match the node's type against `consumes` from list_plugins and call the plugin
   that covers the hop; where nothing installed covers it, say so rather than filling the gap in.

3. REPORT IN FOUR PARTS, always in this order: corroborated as one owner, with the evidence; still a
   candidate, and the specific check that would settle it; ruled out, and why; what nothing
   installed here can reach.

HANDING OFF: when a lead turns into infrastructure — a personal domain, a mail server, an IP in a
header — that is where this pack ends and "Infrastructure pivoting" begins.

sections.summary: From a username: spreading it across platforms.
sections.body:
JUDGE THE CROWD BEFORE THE SWEEP — "corroborate" says how. A dictionary word, a franchise
reference or a leaked-password staple is worn by strangers on every platform: run the sweep if you
like, but say up front that this handle will not group anybody, and do not build a candidate list out
of it. A coined or oddly-spelled string is worth reading every hit of.

THE SWEEP. Run the account-search plugin (WhatsMyName) to enumerate the handle across ~700 sites.
Each hit is a CANDIDATE account — not yet the same person. The hit COUNT is itself evidence about the
crowd: 200 hits across 700 sites is a common string, whatever you assumed before the sweep.

VARIANTS ARE SEARCH INPUTS, NOT FINDINGS. Separators (dev.kim / dev_kim / devkim), trailing digits,
an initial-plus-surname form, a transliteration where the subject writes in another script. One
becomes a node only where a tool returned a hit for it. A variant you composed and could not check
goes in the REPORT — a candidate with what would settle it, or a dead end so nobody repeats it —
never on the canvas, which cannot show whose idea a string was.

MODEL EACH ACCOUNT SEPARATELY. identity.account is username AND platform, so one handle across five
sites is five accounts, and that is correct rather than a duplication to clean up. Stage a node for
each hit with its platform and its SOURCE edge to the profile URL, unconditionally. Hold only the
SAME-PERSON edge, until "corroborate" says you have earned it.

TRIAGE BEFORE YOU READ, AND FAN OUT. A sweep returns more hits than a turn has steps, and reading
them one after another ends the turn before a single pair is corroborated. Rank first: platforms that
carry real identity (code hosting, professional networks, anything with a bio and links) over
throwaway forum registrations, and populated accounts over empty shells. Then hand the survivors to
investigate_in_parallel, one lead each — they are independent, so nothing is lost by working them at
once. "from-profile" says what to take off each one.

FEED BACK IN. Every account carries its own new leads — an address in a bio, a linked site, a variant
used elsewhere. Run each through the section that matches it rather than treating the sweep as the
end of the work.

sections.summary: From an email address: the handles, keys and documents behind it.
sections.body:
An address is four leads at once. Take all four before calling it exhausted.

1. THE LOCAL PART IS A HANDLE. Run it through "from-handle" — most people reuse it. The address
   itself is also worth sweeping, where the account-search plugin accepts one.

2. THE DOMAIN DECIDES WHAT THE ADDRESS IS WORTH. A mainstream provider says nothing about anybody —
   both being on Gmail is not a signal at any quantity. A company or personal domain is a strong
   attribute and a handoff: the domain itself belongs to "Infrastructure pivoting". A DISPOSABLE or
   throwaway provider cuts the other way, and is worth checking where a plugin covers it: two
   accounts sharing a burner address is WEAKER than it looks, because burners are shared, recycled
   and reused by unrelated people.

3. PUBLIC KEY DIRECTORIES. A PGP lookup returns the key's user IDs, which routinely carry a real
   name, an employer address, and OTHER addresses bound to the same key — one of the few genuine
   self-declarations in this whole pack, and machine-readable. Where a key exists its fingerprint is
   a stronger identity than any handle, since it is asserted by the holder rather than chosen.

4. DOCUMENTS AND SHARED OBJECTS. An address that owns or edits a shared document exposes the platform
   account behind it, where a plugin covers that surface. The same goes for anything else that maps
   an address to an account id rather than to a name.

WHAT AN ADDRESS DOES NOT ESTABLISH: that the person controls it, now or ever. An address in a bio was
typed by whoever wrote the bio. Treat it as verified only when a tool observed the platform
confirming it, or when the address itself produced something — a key, a document, a reply.

sections.summary: From one profile page: every pivot it carries.
sections.body:
One profile page is the densest thing in this pack: it carries more independent axes than a sweep
does. Read it with the platform's own plugin where one is installed, fetch_page otherwise, and take
EVERY field — "corroborate" multiplies axes, and each one narrows the population.

  handle, display name       pivots for "from-handle"
  bio text                   addresses, other handles, an employer, a city, a linked site
  linked sites               the strongest thing on the page. A link to another account IS the
                             cross-link that settles a pair — a self-declaration, not an inference
  avatar                     reverse-image it where a plugin covers that. A reused non-default
                             avatar is a real link; a default, a stock image or a popular meme is
                             nothing, however exactly it matches
  numeric / internal id      store it in account.user_id. Display names change and get copied; the
                             id does not. Where the platform's identity IS the id (Telegram),
                             resolve the handle to it and treat THAT as the account
  created date               account.created_date. Weak on its own, and useful mostly for ruling
                             OUT — an account created before the subject existed under that name is
                             somebody else
  posting language, hours    the one axis nobody copies deliberately, which is exactly what makes
                             it independent of everything else on the page

STAGE THE PAGE. One web.url node for the profile, reused for every finding you read there, with the
edge in the same call. A fact with no page behind it cannot be re-checked by anyone, including you.

WHAT THE PAGE IS TODAY IS NOT WHAT IT WAS. An archive or snapshot plugin on the same URL returns
earlier revisions: an old bio naming a previous handle, an address since removed, a link since
deleted. People tidy their profiles, and the pre-tidy version is where the identifying detail
usually still is.

CAUTION: everything on this page was written by the subject, or by whoever is impersonating them.
A whole profile can be copied in ONE act — that is precisely the correlation "corroborate" warns
about, and it is why the id, the timestamps and the posting pattern are worth more than the bio.

sections.summary: A candidate pair with a gap: the check that would settle it.
sections.body:
This is the loop. A candidate pair has a GAP — the one thing that, if you knew it, would settle it.
Name the gap, name the check that produces it, run the check. Never report a gap you were holding a
tool for.

Work from what you NEED, not from what you happen to have:

  the gap                    the check                             where it comes from
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  a shared address           read both bios and contact fields     fetch_page, platform plugin
                             commit / package metadata             a code-hosting account's own
                                                                   commits carry an author address
  a cross-link               read both profiles' link fields       fetch_page
  the same avatar            reverse-image the avatar URL          image plugin
  an earlier name/address    snapshot the profile URL              archive plugin
  a platform identity        resolve the handle to a numeric id    platform plugin
  a real name or employer    the user IDs bound to a public key    PGP lookup on a known address
  an activity pattern        posting times, language, cadence      platform posts plugin
  the base rate itself       a quoted search for the handle        web_search, plus the sweep's
                                                                   own hit count

Where the pack a check needs is not installed, name the check you cannot run: that is part 4 of the
report, and it is worth more to the analyst than a hedged verdict.

PICK THE CHECK THAT SETTLES THE MOST PAIRS. Eight candidates against one subject: reading eight bios
for a shared address settles all eight in one pass, while chasing one pair through four hops settles
one. Breadth first where the check is uniform; depth only on what survives it.

A CHECK THAT COMES BACK EMPTY IS A RESULT. "No address on either profile" is what moves a pair from
open to ruled-out-for-now, and it belongs in the report so that nobody — including you, next turn —
spends the request again.

sections.summary: Judging whether two accounts are one person — how narrow is the population?
sections.body:
Same username is a LEAD. Whether it is more than that is a judgement about ONE quantity:

  IF THESE WERE TWO UNRELATED PEOPLE, HOW LIKELY IS EVERYTHING YOU ARE LOOKING AT?

Equivalently: how many people could produce this whole observation? Estimate it, say what the
estimate rests on, and let the size of the number decide.

STEP 1 — THE CROWD BEHIND EACH ATTRIBUTE. Judge it from what you know about the world; that is what
you are for. What decides it is nearly always one of these, so name WHICH:
  - a cultural source: a lyric, a line of dialogue, a meme, a character, a franchise
  - a leaked-password or wordlist staple (trustno1, letmein) — worn by tens of thousands
  - a dictionary word, a given name, a very short string
  - a naming convention: initials plus digits, a name plus a birth year, a romanised Korean or
    Japanese name — narrow, but not unique
  - a coined word, a misspelling, an unusual compound — effectively unique
Write the reason in one line. "An X-Files line and a perennial top-20 leaked password" is something
the analyst can check and dispute in two seconds. "Common, in my judgement" is not an estimate, it is
a refusal to make one — when you cannot name the kind, MEASURE instead (a quoted search, the sweep's
own hit count) and say that you measured.

STEP 2 — CONDITION ON EVERYTHING ELSE. The crowd that matters is not the crowd behind the handle. It
is the crowd behind the handle AND every other attribute you observed. A globally known album title
may be worn by thousands; worn by someone who is also Korean and also works in IT security, it is
worn by a handful. This is a PRODUCT, and it is the whole reason a judgement beats a scoring table —
the table would have called that three points and stopped.

STEP 3 — CHECK INDEPENDENCE, WHICH IS WHERE THIS GOES WRONG. Axes multiply only where they could not
have come from the same act. The test: DID THEY COME FROM DIFFERENT TOOL RESULTS?
  multiplies       the handle (sweep) x the timezone (commit metadata) x the field (repo contents)
  does NOT         handle x display name x avatar x bio phrasing — one profile copy produces all
                   four at once, and an impersonator produces them the same way
  does NOT         "Korean, in security" read off BOTH bios — one axis observed twice
Then watch for CORRELATION between the attributes themselves. If that album's fandom is concentrated
in one country, nationality is not independent of the handle, it is a consequence of it. Ask what the
attribute looks like AMONG THE PEOPLE WHO SHARE THE HANDLE, not among people in general.

STEP 4 — WHAT A NARROW POPULATION BUYS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It does NOT stage a same-person edge.
That takes a tool result naming both endpoints together — a profile linking to the other account, a
verified address shared by both, a key binding them, a platform field naming one from the other. One
such observation is enough, and nothing else is; that rule is not this pack's to relax. What the
narrowing does buy:
  - the EVIDENCE edges, which go on the canvas now: "shares distinctive handle", "reuses avatar",
    "both operate KR infrastructure". Labelled for what was observed, never "is".
  - the BUDGET. A pair narrowed to a handful of people is worth pushing through "discriminate"; a
    pair still standing at ten thousand is worth dropping, and saying so.
  - the REPORT. "Effectively settled, missing only a self-declaration" is a different sentence from
    "candidate", and sentences are what the analyst actually reads.

BEFORE STAGING A SAME-PERSON EDGE, CHALLENGE IT. Hand the whole evidence bundle to challenge_claim —
an independent second read of the same world knowledge, and where "that handle is actually an anime
character" or "that fandom is 80% Korean" gets to surface. A REFUTED verdict withdraws the edge, and
anything pulled in only to support it. A WEAK one stages nothing and goes into the report with the
skeptic's reasoning attached, so the analyst decides with the counter-argument in front of them.

WHEN YOU CAN NEITHER JUDGE NOR MEASURE — an unfamiliar script, a subculture you do not know, web
access turned off — fall back to counting: three attributes from genuinely different axes, or it
stays a candidate. Say that you fell back, and to what. This is the floor under the judgement, not
the method; reach for it when the judgement is unavailable, not instead of making one.

WORKED EXAMPLES:

  trustno1, on eleven platforms.
  An X-Files line and a perennial top-20 leaked password: tens of thousands of unrelated people, and
  nothing multiplies out of a number that size. Report the sweep, state plainly that this handle
  groups nobody, and do not build a candidate list from it. The correct output is zero pairs.

  whatabeautifulmemory on GitHub and on a security forum.
  A well-known album title — thousands worldwide. But the GitHub account's commit timezone is KST and
  its repositories are exploit tooling, while the forum account posts Korean-language advisories.
  Handle x country x field, each from a different observation: a handful of people. That earns
  "shares distinctive handle" and "both work in KR security" as evidence edges, a challenge_claim
  pass, and the "discriminate" table pointed straight at it — not a same-person edge, yet. What would
  settle it: an address on either side, or one profile linking to the other.

  dev_kim on GitHub and dev_kim on Telegram, both bios saying "Seoul", both created in 2021.
  Kim is among the most common surnames in Korea and dev is a job title: this handle is a convention,
  not a coinage. Seoul is ten million people AND it was read off both bios, so it is one axis rather
  than two. The same creation year is a coincidence, not an axis. Two account nodes, no same-person
  edge, and the gap named: an address, a cross-link, or the GitHub account's commit email — which
  "discriminate" says how to get.

A link you did not draw costs nothing; a wrong one costs the analyst their confidence in everything
else you staged — and you do not get to assume they will see it before it lands. Some cases apply
your changes as you make them, so write every same-person edge as if nobody will check it first.

starters.label: Deep-dive one handle
starters.summary: Spread a single username across platforms, then work out which hits are the same person.
starters.prompt:
I want to deep dive on the user account "{{handle}}".
For your information: {{context}}.
Judge how common the handle is before you sweep and tell me what that judgement rests on. Enumerate where it exists, then use "discriminate" to close the gaps and "corroborate" to separate the accounts that are genuinely one owner from the ones that merely share a name. Say plainly where you are guessing.
Report in the four parts the overview names.

starters.label: Start from an email address
starters.summary: Turn an address into the handles and accounts behind it.
starters.prompt:
Start from the email address {{email}}.
Take all four leads the address carries, find the accounts, and keep each one a candidate until the population behind the shared attributes is narrow enough to say otherwise.
Read "from-email", then "corroborate".

starters.label: Start from a profile page
starters.summary: Mine one profile for the handle, display name, bio and links, then spread from those.
starters.prompt:
Start from this profile: {{url}}.
Pull out everything that identifies the owner — handle, display name, bio, linked sites, avatar, internal id, creation date, posting language — and use each as its own pivot. Record where every detail came from, and treat what you reach as candidates rather than the same person.
Read "from-profile", then "corroborate".

starters.label: Try variants of a handle
starters.summary: For when the obvious spelling is taken, abandoned, or too common to be useful.
starters.prompt:
The handle {{handle}} is probably one of several the same person uses.
Work out the plausible variants — separators, trailing numbers, initial-plus-surname forms, a transliteration of {{native}} — and check those as well as the original.
In your reply, list every variant you tried including the dead ends, so I do not repeat them — a variant nothing could check stays out of the graph.
Read "from-handle" — judge the handle's crowd before the sweep.

starters.label: Expand a person already in the case
starters.summary: Use what the graph already holds about someone as the starting set.
starters.prompt:
Take the person {{person}} as they already exist in this case.
Read the accounts, handles and addresses already attached to them, use each as a pivot, and look for accounts the case has not reached yet. Do not re-stage what is already here — extend it, and say what is new.
Read "corroborate" before extending anything.

variables.label: Person node
variables.placeholder: the account holder in this case

starters.label: Are these the same person?
starters.summary: Test a suspected link between two accounts before it becomes an edge.
starters.prompt:
Decide whether "{{a}}" and "{{b}}" belong to the same person.
Read "corroborate" first, and show me the estimate rather than a verdict: how large is the crowd behind each shared attribute and what does that rest on, what is left once you condition on all of them together, and which of those attributes are genuinely independent observations rather than one profile copied. Then tell me what would actually settle it — and do not draw a same-person edge on a shared handle alone.

starters.label: Sort candidates by how well they hold up
starters.summary: A pile of hits from an enumeration run, separated into corroborated, unproven, and ruled out.
starters.prompt:
These are candidate accounts for one person: {{candidates}}.
Sort them into three groups — corroborated as the same owner, plausible but unproven, and ruled out — and for every one name the specific evidence that put it there. Where a group is large, run the single check that moves the most of them rather than telling me about it.
Read "corroborate" to sort, then "discriminate" to close the gaps.

variables.label: Candidate accounts
variables.placeholder: one per line, or "everything staged in this case"

starters.label: Test a suspected sock-puppet set
starters.summary: Several accounts, one suspected operator — what actually ties them together?
starters.prompt:
These accounts are suspected to be operated by one person: {{accounts}}.
Look for what would actually establish common control — shared recovery details, cross-links, reused rare text or avatars, creation patterns, posting rhythm. Report per pair, not for the set as a whole, because one strong pair does not make the rest of the set real.
Read "corroborate" and estimate the population per PAIR.

starters.label: Rule out a false match
starters.summary: Deliberately try to break a link the case is leaning on.
starters.prompt:
I suspect {{a}} and {{b}} are NOT the same person, despite what they appear to share.
Argue that case as strongly as the evidence allows: how large is the crowd behind the shared attribute, and what would you expect to see if they really were one person that is absent here? Then argue the other side, and tell me which is better supported.
Read "corroborate".

starters.label: Summarise what the case establishes
starters.summary: Corroborated, candidate and ruled out — each conclusion tied to the evidence it rests on.
starters.prompt:
Summarise what this case now establishes about {{subject}}.
Separate what is corroborated from what is still a candidate and what has been ruled out, and tie every conclusion to the node or edge it rests on. Where a conclusion rests on one piece of evidence, say so — that is the part most likely to be wrong.
Report in the four parts the overview names.

variables.label: Who or what the summary is about

starters.label: What would settle the open questions?
starters.summary: Turn the unresolved parts of the case into a list of specific next checks.
starters.prompt:
Go over what is unresolved in this case and turn it into next steps.
For each open question name the specific evidence that would settle it and the check that would produce that evidence. Run the ones this project's installed plugins can actually answer rather than listing them, and say plainly which ones nothing here can reach.
Read "discriminate", and report in the four parts the overview names.
